§ Intro

Two questions, two tools

Nearly every question you ask of a big sheet is one of these two. Each has its own one-click tool, and this deck teaches both. No formulas needed anywhere in this lesson.

"Which is biggest? Who comes first?"
→ SORT

Rearranges every row into an order you choose: largest to smallest, A to Z, oldest to newest. The answer floats to the top.

"Show me only…"
→ FILTER

Hides every row you don't want to see right now: one council, one month, everything over a number. The rest waits quietly out of sight.

Neither tool changes your numbers. Sort rearranges rows; filter hides rows. Both are reversible.
sort answers ranking questions filter answers "just show me this slice" questions and used together they answer almost anything — that combo closes the deck
§ Intro

Meet the dataset

NT Cyber Pulse 2026 — a door-to-door survey of Top End households: what device people carry, and how they look after their accounts. All numbers are synthetic, built for practice. On screen we work with 9 suburbs you can see whole; the practice workbook has the full sheet, 58 suburbs.

🌏 Top End Survey — as it arrived: no particular order
Two columns to watch: Shares pwd counts people whose password is shared or written down; No MFA counts people with no second lock on their accounts. Someone has to decide which suburbs need help first.
§ Sort basics

Before anything: the one-cell rule

The single most important habit in this whole deck. Don't select anything. Just click one cell in the column you care about.

1. One click, one cell. That's your entire selection.
2. Excel finds the edges of your data block by itself: every joined-up row and column, top to bottom.
3. It also recognises row 1 as headers and keeps them parked at the top.
click any cell in the column you want to sort by — here, Shares pwd no dragging, no highlighting; Excel takes the whole table from that one click headers stay put; only the data rows will move
Never highlight a whole column and then sort. That sorts one column on its own and scrambles your rows. The trap gets its own slide later.

§ Sort basics

Rows travel together

The worry everyone has the first time: "won't sorting mix up my numbers?" Watch one suburb through a sort.

Before — survey order
After — sorted by Shares pwd, largest first
watch Casuarina: it starts on row 6, with 510 surveyed, 199 shared, 265 no MFA after the sort it sits on row 2 — and every one of its numbers came with it
A sort moves whole rows. Suburbs never swap numbers. That is exactly why you click one cell instead of selecting a column.

§ The Sort dialog

The sort safety net

Three things worth knowing before you sort anything that matters.

The warning box is your friend

If you did select a column and hit sort, Excel throws a lifeline:

Sort Warning✕

Microsoft Excel found data next to your selection.

Expand the selection Continue with the current selection
Sort…Cancel

→ always take Expand the selection

Blank rows and columns split the data

Excel finds the edges of your data by walking outward until it hits emptiness. A fully blank row or column inside your table is an edge: everything past it gets left out of the sort.

Keep your table one solid block; delete decorative blank rows.

Ctrl+Z is the escape hatch

A sort has no Clear button; the old order is simply gone. But Ctrl+Z straight after undoes it perfectly.

Sorted something weird and kept working? You can still press Ctrl+Z several times, or close the file without saving.

§ The Sort dialog

The header trap: one clean header row

Sorting behaves only when row 1 is headers and everything under it is data. Some sheets keep a second row of notes or question wording under the headers, and that's where sorts go wrong.

row 2 here isn't data — it's the survey question wording, parked under the headers sort the sheet and Excel treats that row as data: it dives in and files itself among the answers on a 1,000-row sheet you might never notice — press Ctrl+Z the moment a sort looks wrong
The rule: one header row, then data, nothing else in the block. Notes and question wording belong on their own sheet. The practice workbook's Survey Responses sheet has exactly this trap waiting; you'll meet it in the final challenge.

Hidden, not deleted

The most important sentence about filtering: the other rows still exist. They are folded away, not thrown away.

status bar ▸3 of 9 records found
The six hidden rows are still in the file: still saved, still counted by totals on other sheets, still there for whoever opens the workbook next. A filter only changes what you can see.

§ Filter

Filters stack

Filter more than one column at once and each funnel narrows the view further. The question: big suburbs, in Darwin only.

status bar ▸5 of 9 records found
first funnel: Surveyed greater than 300 leaves five suburbs second funnel: Council = Darwin narrows those five to three; both funnels work at once the answer: Nightcliff, Casuarina and Karama are Darwin's big suburbs
Every funnelled header is filtering at the same time. Clear them one at a time from each column's arrow menu, or all at once with Data ▸ Clear.
§ Filter

Three ways back to everything

Filters are polite: every one of them is reversible, at three different scales.

Clear one column

The arrow menu of a filtered column offers:

Clear Filter From "Council"

The other funnels keep working; only this column lets go.

Clear every filter

Data ▸ Sort & Filter ▸ Clear releases all columns at once. Every row returns; the ▾ arrows stay, ready for next time.

Switch filtering off

Data ▸ Filter again — the same funnel button that turned it on. Arrows disappear, all rows return, the sheet is back to plain.

Worth knowing: filters save with the file. Leave one on and the next person opens a workbook that looks half empty; clear filters before you save and share.

§ Trip-ups

When it goes wrong — the five usual suspects

"My rows got scrambled"

You selected a column (or part of one) and sorted just that. One column reordered on its own; every row now mixes suburbs.

Fix: Ctrl+Z immediately. Next time: click one cell, and if the Sort Warning appears, choose Expand the selection.

"10 sorted before 9"

Numbers stored as text sort letter by letter, so "10" files before "9". Tell-tales: left-aligned numbers and small green corner marks.

Fix: select the column, use the warning marker's Convert to Number, then sort again.

"Half my data is missing"

A leftover filter, almost every time; possibly one that arrived saved inside the file.

Fix: look for blue skipping row numbers and funnel icons; then Data ▸ Clear.

"The sort ignored some rows"

A fully blank row or column inside the table split it into two blocks, and Excel only sorted the block you clicked in.

Fix: delete blank rows and columns inside the data, then sort again.

"There's a header in my data"

A second header row, notes, or question wording sat inside the block and got sorted like data.

Fix: Ctrl+Z, move notes to their own sheet, keep one clean header row.

Golden rule

One clean header row, one solid block of data, one click in one cell. Do that and sort and filter behave every single time.

§ Wrap

The one-slide cheat sheet

Where everything lives

  • Data tab ▸ Sort & Filter group — all of it
  • A to Z / Z to A — one-column sort
  • Sort — the dialog, for two-level sorts
  • Filter — the funnel; arrows on / off
  • Clear — release every filter at once
  • Right-click a cell ▸ Sort / Filter works too

Which tool for which question

Who's highest, lowest, first?Sort
Show me only this councilFilter
Everything over a numberNumber Filters
Order by two things at onceSort dialog
Rank inside one sliceFilter, then sort

Remember

  • Click one cell; never select a column
  • A sort moves whole rows
  • Filtering hides, it never deletes
  • Blue skipping row numbers = filter is on
  • Ctrl+Z undoes a sort straight away
  • One clean header row, no notes in the block
  • Clear filters before you save and share

§ Wrap

Now do it for real

Download the practice workbook and open the Top End Survey sheet: the full version of what you've been using, 58 suburbs, real column names (Shares passwords, No MFA).

Your six talking points

  1. One cell, one click — never select a column before sorting.
  2. Sort rearranges whole rows — largest to smallest, A to Z; the answer floats to the top.
  3. The Sort dialog stacks rules: by council, then by the number that matters.
  4. Filter hides, never deletes — checkboxes for names, Number Filters for "over 200".
  5. Read the tell-tales — blue skipping row numbers, funnel icons, the status bar count.
  6. Filter, then sort — narrow to the slice, then rank it. That combo answers real questions.
